title: Arrays & Linked Lists
tagline: Two fundamental ways to store a sequence — and why the tradeoff changes everything about speed.

sections.content:
Arrays and linked lists are the two foundational sequence structures. They both hold ordered collections of elements, yet they make opposite bets: arrays pay upfront for **contiguous memory** to win O(1) random access, while linked lists scatter nodes freely to win O(1) insertion and deletion. Every higher-level structure — stacks, queues, hash tables, even some trees — is built on top of one (or both) of these primitives.

JavaScript's built-in `Array` is a **dynamic array** — it hides a fixed-size memory block behind an API that auto-resizes. Understanding what happens under that hood (the occasional O(n) copy, the amortised O(1) append) is exactly what interviewers probe when they ask about time complexity.

sections.title: Reserved Cinema Seats vs a Treasure Hunt
sections.content:
Imagine a cinema with numbered seats. You book seats 10–19 — ten consecutive slots. To reach seat 14 you walk straight there: *start + offset*. That is an **array**: contiguous, numbered, randomly accessible in one step.

Now picture a treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the next clue is hidden. You must follow the chain from clue 1 to reach clue 7 — no shortcuts. That is a **linked list**: each element (node) holds its value and a pointer to the next node. Inserting a new clue between clue 3 and clue 4 is trivial — update two pointers. But inserting a seat into the middle of the cinema row forces everyone to shift over.

A **static array** is a contiguous block of memory. Because each element occupies the same fixed number of bytes, the CPU computes `address = base + i × element_size` in one arithmetic step — O(1) random access regardless of array size. The catch: the size must be declared upfront. Need more space? Allocate a new block and copy everything — O(n).

**Dynamic arrays** (JavaScript `Array`, Python `list`, Java `ArrayList`) hide this behind automatic resizing. When the buffer fills, the runtime allocates a new buffer — typically 2× the current capacity — and copies all elements. Because the buffer doubles exponentially, resizing happens increasingly rarely. Total copy work across *n* appends stays below 2n, so the **amortised cost of appending is O(1)**. Insertion or deletion in the middle is still O(n) because elements must shift.

A **singly linked list** stores each element in a node with `value` and `next` fields. Nodes can live anywhere on the heap — no contiguous layout required. Inserting a node between two existing nodes rewires two pointers: O(1) *once you hold a reference*. Getting that reference requires walking from the head: O(n). A **doubly linked list** adds a `prev` pointer, enabling O(1) deletion by reference without tracking the predecessor — the trick used by browser LRU caches and JavaScript engine task queues.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Storing a `tail` pointer upgrades `append` from O(n) to O(1) — a critical optimisation that is often missed in first implementations. `insertAt` still pays O(n) to walk to the position; once there, the rewiring is O(1). This asymmetry is the core tradeoff of linked lists.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Interview tip — reverse a linked list in-place:** Use three pointers (`prev = null`, `cur = head`, `next`). In each iteration: save `next = cur.next`, flip `cur.next = prev`, advance both. O(n) time, O(1) space. This is one of the most-asked linked list questions because it tests pointer thinking, not value thinking.

items: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, giving O(1) random access via index arithmetic (`base + i × size`).
Dynamic arrays amortise O(n) copy cost by doubling buffer size on overflow — appending is O(1) amortised.
Linked list nodes hold a value and a `next` pointer; index access is O(n) but inserting/deleting with a reference is O(1).
Doubly linked lists add a `prev` pointer enabling O(1) deletion by reference — used in LRU caches and task queues.
Choose arrays for random access and cache-friendly iteration; choose linked lists for frequent O(1) insertions and deletions at known positions.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of accessing element at index `i` in a static array?
quiz.explanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory. The CPU computes `base + i × element_size` in one arithmetic step — O(1) regardless of array size.

quiz.question: Why does appending to a JavaScript Array have O(1) amortised complexity despite occasional O(n) copies?
options: JavaScript engines use a hash map instead of contiguous memory
The buffer doubles on overflow so copies happen exponentially rarely
JavaScript Array uses a linked list under the hood
The garbage collector handles copying asynchronously
quiz.explanation: When the buffer fills, a 2× buffer is allocated and all elements copied. Because the buffer doubles, total copy work across n appends is less than 2n — O(1) amortised per append.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of prepending (inserting at head) a node in a singly linked list?
quiz.explanation: Prepending creates a new node, points its `next` to the current head, then updates head — three pointer operations independent of list length.

quiz.question: You hold a direct reference to a node in a doubly linked list. What is the deletion time complexity?
options: O(1) — update prev and next pointers only
quiz.explanation: The `prev` pointer gives direct access to the predecessor. Removal updates `node.prev.next` and `node.next.prev` — two pointer writes, O(1).

quiz.question: Which operation is O(n) on a dynamic array but O(1) on a singly linked list (head access)?
quiz.explanation: Inserting at the front of a dynamic array shifts every element right — O(n). Prepending to a linked list updates only the head pointer — O(1).

quiz.question: What memory disadvantage does a doubly linked list have compared to an array of the same integers?
options: Elements must be stored in sorted order
Each node stores two extra pointer fields (prev and next)
Doubly linked lists cannot store duplicate values
Maximum size is fixed at creation
quiz.explanation: Each node stores value + prev + next. On a 64-bit system each pointer is 8 bytes, so a doubly linked list of integers uses roughly 3× the memory of a plain array of the same values.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of `Array.prototype.unshift(value)` in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: `unshift` shifts every existing element one index right to create space at index 0 — touching all n elements, O(n).

quiz.question: In a singly linked list with no tail pointer, what is the time complexity of appending to the back?
quiz.explanation: Without a tail pointer you must traverse from head to the last node before linking the new node — visiting every existing node, O(n).

quiz.question: Which is the correct formula for computing the memory address of element `i` in an array with base address B and element size S?
quiz.explanation: `B + i × S` accounts for the base offset plus i full-sized elements before index i. This single arithmetic step is why array access is O(1).

quiz.question: You are building a feed where new posts are always added to the top and users scroll sequentially. Which structure is most appropriate?
options: Static array — O(1) access by index
Singly linked list with head and tail pointers — O(1) prepend, sequential read
Binary search tree — O(log n) insert
quiz.explanation: New posts prepend in O(1). Users scroll sequentially, which linked list traversal handles well. A dynamic array would pay O(n) on every prepend to shift existing elements.
